articles.title: EU's Cyber Resilience Act starts the 24-hour vulnerability clock
articles.text: Manufacturers selling products with digital elements in the EU must now report actively exploited vulnerabilities to cybersecurity authorities under the Cyber Resilience Act's mandatory reporting rules. The reporting duties set out in Article 14 of the CRA became applicable today. Subject to the regulation's exemptions, they apply to manufacturers of products with digital elements made available in the EU, regardless of where those manufacturers are based. Manufacturers must submit an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability, followed by a more detailed notification within 72 hours. The same deadlines apply to severe incidents affecting the security of products with digital elements. The only difference in timing is related to the final report. Manufacturers must provide a final report on an actively exploited vulnerability within 14 days of making a corrective or mitigating measure available. For serious incidents, the final report is due one month after the first report. Darren Anstee, CTO for security at Netscout, said the reporting deadlines introduce much-needed urgency in working toward global cyber resilience. "The 24-hour window in which an initial warning must be reported creates a level of urgency, with subsequent deadlines ensuring that the gathering and release of additional information is prompt," he said. "Better, more rapid sharing of information helps organisations put defences and mitigating controls in place when they know there is heightened risk." EU and non-EU manufacturers must file these reports through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform (SRP). Notifications are addressed to the coordinating computer security incident response team (CSIRT) determined under the CRA. For an EU manufacturer, this is generally the CSIRT for the member state where it has its main establishment; separate rules determine the coordinator for manufacturers based outside the bloc. Manufacturers must also inform affected users, where appropriate, about actively exploited vulnerabilities or severe incidents. The CRA states that users must be informed of available corrections or mitigations without undue delay. Generally, failures under the CRA are punishable by varying tiers of fines, the most serious of which can reach €15 million ($17.4 million) or 2.5 percent of the offender's annual turnover, whichever is higher. The reporting duties that took effect today are classified as core responsibilities under the act, meaning failures to comply with them could lead to the maximum fines being issued. They are the latest step in the EU's plan to drip-feed tighter security regulations on companies operating in the bloc. Most remaining CRA provisions become applicable on December 11, 2027, at which time manufacturers will also be required to embed security by design and default. That means no default passwords and security updates are no longer optional. Products covered by the CRA will also have to undergo the applicable conformity assessment before being placed on the EU market and bearing a CE mark. More than a deadline The CRA's new rules are not just intended to accelerate manufacturers' responses to security flaws. They are also intended to give businesses a better understanding of their software supply chains. With the reporting clock starting as soon as manufacturers become aware of an issue, they cannot afford to begin mapping an affected product only after a vulnerability or incident emerges. They need a comprehensive view of the affected product and any related products that may share the flaw if they are to meet the deadlines. Furthermore, those requirements demand that manufacturers maintain this understanding throughout each product's lifecycle. Creating a software bill of materials (SBOM) when a product is launched is one thing. The SBOM becomes a mandatory requirement when most of the CRA's remaining provisions become applicable next year. Maintaining that security snapshot over time, however, is intended to help reduce the number and impact of serious cyberattacks across the EU. "What all this means for manufacturers is that secure development, effective vulnerability handling, and traceability across the software supply chain should be elevated to the top of their priority list," said Eran Kinsbruner, veep of product marketing at Checkmarx. "Modern applications are assembled from a complex ecosystem of components, with combinations of proprietary code, open-source packages, third-party components and, increasingly, AI models and services all interconnected," he added. "Organizations need to understand these components, their dependencies and the risks they introduce." Given enough time, the CRA looks set to improve cyber resilience across the board. However, lawyers warn that manufacturers, particularly those outside heavily regulated sectors, must now contend with a growing body of overlapping rules. "The CRA is arriving as organizations are already grappling with a growing body of Digital Decade legislation, including NIS2, DORA, the Data Act, and the AI Act," said Heidi Waem, data, privacy and cybersecurity partner at DLA Piper. "We're seeing the compliance challenge for many businesses evolving beyond understanding single regulations in isolation, but determining how multiple frameworks interact, where requirements overlap and how compliance programmes can be coordinated across them." John Magee, partner and global co-chair of data, privacy, and cybersecurity at the same law firm, added: "Even now we're seeing the breadth of the regulation's reach catching organizations off guard. "Many still associate the CRA primarily with consumer IoT devices, when in reality it applies to a much broader pool of products with digital elements. For compliance teams already very busy managing multiple Digital Decade initiatives, there is a risk that this first wave of CRA obligations has arrived sooner, and with a wider impact, than they had expected." ®
articles.summary: Manufacturers selling products with digital elements in the EU must now report actively exploited vulnerabilities to cybersecurity authorities under the Cyber Resilience Act's mandatory reporting rule

articles.title: ‘Society as battlefield’: NATO cites Indian military paper on cognitive warfare. What it says
articles.text:
New Delhi: An Indian research paper on how the human brain is the next site of modern warfare and the battlefield now social has been used as a reference for a publication on hybrid warfare co-funded by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).
In a seminal work, former Indian military officers Lt. Gen. D.S. Hooda and Lt. Col. Pavithran Rajan put forth a framework to approach cognitive warfare known as STCB—Socio-Technical-Cognitive Battlespace—which places social structures, technology and human cognition at the centre of strategic analysis. “In modern warfare, societies themselves have become battlefields,” the paper says.
The paper, titled ‘Beyond the Kinetic: Deconstructing Warfare in the Socio-Technical-Cognitive Battlespace’, was written in January 2026 and used the Russia-Ukraine war to establish how “strategic success and national resilience increasingly depend on the capacity to comprehend, adapt to, and leverage the intricate dynamics binding social cohesion, technical infrastructure, and cognitive influence into an integrated whole”.
The framework was cited in the Polish Association for National Security’s monograph, ‘Hybrid War: Threats to Power Grid Infrastructure’, which had a similar argument that a state can be weakened without its adversary first destroying its armies or occupying its cities. It simply needs to work around the mind to influence society.
The Polish volume, written by political scientists Jarosław Tomasiewicz and Michal Piekarski and defence studies expert Marcin Lipka, attempts to look at how hybrid warfare is evolving rapidly alongside artificial intelligence, cyberoperations and increasingly interconnected societies.
Their central argument by the Polish authors is that hybrid warfare is moving toward what they describe as ‘algorithmic warfare’. In this conception, artificial intelligence acts as a force multiplier, allowing adversaries to identify vulnerabilities, generate tailored messages, distribute them at scale and adjust campaigns in response to their effects.
The objective is no longer simply to destroy an opponent’s physical capabilities. It is to disrupt the systems through which a society perceives events, makes decisions and maintains confidence in its institutions. Ukraine is presented as an important laboratory for understanding these changes.
Hooda and Rajan’s paper for Indian think tanks, the Council for Strategic and Defense Research (CSDR) and Centre for Land Warfare Studies (CLAWS), puts forward the same argument.
“The rapid advance of digital technologies, deeply ingrained in modern life, is having a decisive effect on the conduct of warfare. Interactions across social, technical, and cognitive domains, mediated by an algorithmic substrate—the underlying layer of codes, data, and platform governance that selects, ranks, routes, and optimizes information flows—now constitute a new battlespace as consequential as any physical terrain,” it says.
Also Read: Not just Su-57: What is on President Putin’s defence agenda as he visits India
The STCB framework
Rajan and Hooda in their paper detail three core components of the STCB framework. First is the social domain, with shared identities, trust networks, collective narratives, and the fault lines that can fracture them. Its subcomponents include cultural narratives and historical memory, social networks and trust, public opinion and political will, identity/group dynamics and societal fault lines, and governance/institutional legitimacy.
Then comes the technical domain with cyber capabilities, Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning, data analytics, communication platforms, and surveillance/sensing technologies that enable warfare and control over the platforms themselves and not just activity on them, which the report frames as a key source of strategic advantage. A key example they cite is Musk’s Starlink being provided to Ukraine.
And the third is what they call the ‘ultimate nerve centre’ — the mental processes of perception, belief, decision-making, and meaning construction. Its mechanisms include perception/meaning management, targeting of cognitive biases, disinformation/misinformation/malinformation, attacks on the adversary’s Observe, Orient, Decide, and Act (OODA) loop, and psychological operations (PsyOps).
These three domains are bound together by what the report calls the algorithmic substrate which is the underlying layer of platforms, models, and control policies that determines who sees what, when, and with what credibility. The report is careful to note this substrate isn’t a fourth domain in the same sense as the other three, but rather the connective ‘nervous system’ that mediates how the social, technical, and cognitive domains interact recursively with one another.
The framework also draws on the OODA loop developed by the American strategist John Boyd, something that the Polish paper cites in detail in one of its chapters. Cognitive warfare, the paper argues, aims to attack the adversary’s OODA loop directly by ‘injecting disinformation and ambiguity (affecting Observe), exploiting cultural biases (affecting Orient), and inducing uncertainty (affecting Decide)’, which allows an attacker to slow or even paralyse an opponent’s decision-making process.
‘The aim is not merely to alter what people think, but to fundamentally reshape how they think, reason, and act,” the paper says.
Both the paper and the monograph then end with how democratic governments, military organisations and even private entities can use the shifting trends in warfare to be better equipped. It’s no longer predicting weapons but about predicting vulnerabilities and the panic it produces in a country or region as a whole and the tools that use narrative warfare.
Democratic governments can make strategies without waddling into propaganda. According to Hooda and Rajan, governments should have a threat assessment framework, national objectives, resource allocation and institutional mechanisms to address this.
The Polish paper argues the same. “The foundation of national security against asymmetric conflicts is and will invariably remain societal resilience and the nation’s capacity to absorb crises without falling into paralysis. The state must continuously shape civic attitudes based on vigilance, solidarity, and trust in legitimate public institutions…without renouncing their essence, namely civil liberties, with freedom of speech at the forefront.”
It is what the Polish paper cites with British historian Mark Galeotti’s quote: “The ‘good guys’ […] can use the same tools just as effectively as the ‘bad guys’.”
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

articles.title: 4 Agniveers questioned after AK-203 assault rifles, pistols, ammo stolen from Madras Regiment armoury
articles.text:
New Delhi: In a major security breach, four AK-203 assault rifles, six 9 mm pistols and an INSAS rifle along with ammunition were stolen from the armoury of the Indian Army’s Madras Regiment in Secunderabad Sunday evening.
The Malkajgiri Police Commissionerate has detained four Agniveers from the premises for questioning after an FIR was registered Monday, based on a complaint from the Indian Army. The case was lodged under sections including 331(4) (lurking house-trespass or house-breaking) and 305 (theft in special protected places) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, it is learnt.
However, officials maintained that they have been rounded up only for questioning on grounds of suspicion and no formal arrests have been made yet.
Apart from the arms, the Army informed the police that around 1,800 rounds of ammunition and 21 magazines were missing from the armoury, putting the entire Bollarum cantonment region in Secunderabad on high alert. Nearly 700 of those missing rounds were of AK-203 rifles.
A statement from Malkajgiri Police Commissioner B. Sumathi is awaited regarding the status of the probe into this case.
According to the sources in the police, army personnel posted with the 20 Madras Regiment alerted the police that around a dozen weapons had gone missing from the armoury.
The armoury was last checked and accounted for Sunday evening. However, on Monday morning, army personnel assigned to oversee arms and ammunition at the Bollarum premises found that the locks of the boxes carrying the weapons and ammo had been forcefully opened.
Sources said all CCTV cameras in the premises were being checked.
In his complaint to the local police, a lieutenant colonel-ranked officer posted with the Madras Regiment informed local authorities that after the fact of missing weapons and ammunition came to light, several steps, such as thorough verification of the complete weapon and ammunition holdings and accounting documents, were carried out.
Additonally, the Army had also carried out identification and questioning of the personnel having access to the storage area.
The facts about missing weapons and ammunition were also intimated to the chain of command, the officer said in his complaint, adding that a detailed internal inquiry was also initiated to find out the circumstances leading to the loss of weapons and ammunition.
However, he urged the police to register a criminal case as well, considering the possibility of “unauthorised possession, misuse or movement” of those missing service weapons and ammunition.
“In view of the nature of the missing articles, particularly the service weapons and ammunition, there is a possibility of their unauthorised possession, misuse or movement. As such, they requested that the matter may kindly be investigated by the Police and an FIR be registered under the applicable provisions relating to theft/misappropriation, unauthorised possession of arms/ammunition and other offences as may be established during investigation,” the Army officer said in his police complaint.
“The unit will provide all available records and extend full cooperation to the investigating agency. Details of missing/stolen weapons/control stores and ammunition, including registration numbers, specifications, relevant accounting documents and particulars of persons having authorised access, shall be furnished to the Investigation Officer. It is requested that necessary action may please be initiated urgently and that appropriate measures may be taken for tracing/recovery of the missing weapons and ammunition and identifying the persons responsible.”
This is an updated version of the report.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)

articles.title: Makkah defence pact now in effect—Secretariat in Riyadh, Pakistani will be 1st Secretary General
articles.text:
New Delhi: Turkey has announced that the Mecca pact’s first secretary general will be from Pakistan and the grouping will be called the Makkah Defence Alliance, with a secretariat in Riyadh.
The announcements were made Monday by Turkey’s foreign minister Hakan Fidan, after the grouping’s first Strategic Political and Defence Committee meeting in Istanbul earlier in the day. This marked their first formal gathering since the three countries signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on 7 August.
Fidan also said the three member states had agreed to begin establishing the grouping’s institutional structure, including a permanent secretariat in Riyadh.
“There is a secretariat that has been established in Riyadh, and the first secretary general will be appointed from amongst our Pakistani brothers,” he said in Turkish at a news conference after the meeting. Adding, “As of today, we have started the process of establishing the institutional structure of the alliance.”
Minister of Foreign Affairs @HakanFidan attended the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee, established under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, in İstanbul with the participation of Yaşar Güler, Minister of National Defence and General Selçuk… pic.twitter.com/ALWrEJhzpp
— Turkish MFA (@MFATurkiye) August 31, 2026
Fidan also said that during the meeting, decisions were taken on “how and when to begin institutionalisation and all our brothers expressed views”.
“For the future of a secure, stable and prosperous region, this alliance is based on international principles such as respecting the sovereignty of other states, territorial integrity and not intervening in internal affairs,” he said.
Fidan also said the grouping would be open to other countries, although prospective members would have to meet conditions, rules and standards yet to be specified.
The alliance, he said, was not directed against any particular country. Instead, its stated principles include respect for national sovereignty, territorial integrity and non-interference in domestic affairs. “We will closely cooperate with friendly countries, and we will continue coordinating our efforts,” Fidan added.
He suggested that the grouping was expected to expand, but cautioned that its institutional mechanisms must be made functional before new members could be incorporated. “If an ally wants to join, the alliance should be functional in a proper manner by then,” he said.
Pakistan was represented at the meeting by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and Field Marshal Asim Munir, who is also the country’s chief of army and defence forces. Turkey was represented by Fidan, Defence Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of the General Staff General Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu. Saudi Arabia was represented by Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and chief of staff General Fayyad bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili.
Fidan clarified that the pact also does not supersede the three countries’ existing international commitments.
The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed on 7 August, contains a mutual defence provision under which the three countries agreed to regard an armed attack against any one member as an attack against all three.
Fidan said the lack of trust and effective security arrangements among countries in the region had contributed to instability and the Makkah Defence Alliance was intended to help fill that gap while presenting itself as a framework for regional security rather than as a bloc aimed at a particular adversary.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)
